evidence_add.extracted: Online Appendix A (added by the 2026 corrigendum): the treatment indicator marks, for each state and month, whether legal fentanyl test strips were available in a way the authors judged capable of a meaningful policy shock; for most jurisdictions the date is the statute's effective date as in the NPHL database (cited there as Davis et al., 2022), and for five the authors depart from it. Table A1, source date and date used: Alabama June 1, 2022, untreated through 2022 (enforcement and pharmacy uncertainty: an Alabama drug threat assessment from 2023 describing legalization as pending, and a pharmacist survey that Table A1 places in 2025, in which 25.2% believed strips were still illegal); Minnesota July 1, 2021, untreated (state law keeps cities' power to ban paraphernalia; two cities named); New Mexico May 18, 2022, untreated (distribution still an offence; implementing rules effective November 29, 2022); North Carolina 2019, treated from July 22, 2022, three years after enactment (a narrow statute; a March–May 2022 pharmacist survey found two pharmacies dispensing strips); District of Columbia April 11, 2019, treated from August 2019 (overlapping emergency, temporary and permanent laws; a local organization's August 2019 statement that the framework was complete as of May 2019). Virginia (July 1, 2019) and West Virginia (June 10, 2022) keep the source's dates after review, as do all states the appendix does not discuss. The authors write that reasonable researchers may reach different judgments. No results with the source's dates are reported, and the six jurisdictions shaded legal on the paper's map without a date (Alaska, Massachusetts, Michigan, New York, Vermont, Wyoming) are not mentioned.
